messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Vinh's Recurrence

Vinh was thirty-four when the two men cornered him in the parking garage behind the hospital where he worked as a chaplain. It was a Tuesday evening in March, nearly two years ago, and he had stayed late to sit with a dying patient's family. The garage was half-empty, fluorescent lights casting long shadows between the concrete pillars. He was walking toward his car when he heard the footsteps quicken behind him—two sets, closing in fast. One of them had a knife. They wanted his wallet, his phone, his watch. When he hesitated, one of them grabbed his collar and slammed him against the pillar. The other pressed the blade against his ribs and told him to stop being stupid. Vinh remembered the smell of stale cigarettes and something chemical—maybe cologne, maybe sweat—and the sound of his own breathing, ragged and panicked, competing with their harsh commands. They took everything. He was not seriously injured, but the violation left him hollowed out in a way the bruises never quite explained.

In the weeks after, Vinh had tried to return to his chaplaincy work. But something had shifted. When he walked through the hospital corridors now, particularly the parking garage, his body would tense. He began noticing people—really noticing them, assessing them. Anyone who vaguely resembled one of his attackers would trigger a cascade of images: the knife, the hand at his collar, the blur of the pillar rushing toward his face. These were not fleeting thoughts; they were vivid, intrusive pictures that flooded his awareness with photographic clarity. The visual memories came unbidden, especially when he encountered men in crowds or in confined spaces like the garage. Over time, Vinh had come to believe that the event had revealed something true about himself—that he was the kind of person who invited predation, who lacked the instinct to protect himself or to read danger correctly. If he had been more alert, more assertive, more like other men, he would have seen them coming. Somebody else would have fought back or run. This conviction, once formed, began to color how he interpreted every reminder of the attack. When he caught sight of someone who resembled one of the men, or when he found himself in a crowded place, that negative appraisal would activate first: *I am the sort of person this happens to.* And immediately, the sensory memories would flood in—the smell, the images, the feeling of helplessness.

The heaviness of these appraisals deepened his isolation. Vinh became convinced that he could not stop bad things from happening to him, that some essential fragility had been exposed. This belief made him hypervigilant in ways that exhausted him. He began avoiding the hospital parking garage entirely, taking the long route through the main entrance even in bad weather. He avoided crowded spaces—the hospital cafeteria, the chapel during services, even the grocery store on weekends. But avoidance only seemed to sharpen his sensitivity. When he did encounter a crowded place—unavoidably, at a colleague's funeral reception—the press of bodies around him triggered both the intrusive images and a surge of rage so intense it frightened him. He could feel the old smell in his nostrils, see the faces looming, and underneath it all was a burning fury at himself for being the kind of man this could happen to, for being powerless. The rage and the images fed each other; remembering the event flooded him with anger at his own perceived weakness, and that anger seemed to sharpen the sensory details even further.

His wife, Maya, had died of cancer just eight months before the mugging. Vinh had been grieving, but functional—his chaplaincy work had given him purpose in that darkness. After the attack, he found himself unable to access even that solace. He stopped attending the hospital's informal support groups. He began calling in sick. The one person who might have helped him carry this—Maya—was already gone. He sat alone in their apartment most evenings now, and when he closed his eyes, he could smell the garage, see the knife, feel the rage at himself for being so utterly, irredeemably powerless. It was this combination—the vivid, intrusive memories; the conviction that he was fundamentally flawed; the certainty that he could not protect himself from harm—that finally brought him to seek help. He was afraid that without intervention, he would disappear entirely into the narrow, controlled world he had built to avoid triggering the cycle again. What he hoped for, though he barely dared articulate it, was to feel like a chaplain again rather than a victim, and to believe that not all bad things were inevitable consequences of who he was.
